title: Fiber Definition
content: The fiber `fiberAt f j` is the set of people assigned to day `j` by the birthday assignment `f`. Formally, it is the filter of `Finset.univ` by the predicate `f i = j`. This is the fundamental building block: a k-way coincidence occurs when some fiber has cardinality at least `k`.

title: k-Way Coincidence Predicate
content: The predicate `HasKWay f k` asserts that assignment `f` has a k-way coincidence: some day `j` has at least `k` people assigned to it. This existential formulation is the natural generalization of the classical birthday collision (k=2). The definition is parameterized by both the assignment and the threshold, enabling uniform treatment of all coincidence levels.

title: Fiber Partition of Unity
content: Proves that fiber sizes sum to the total population: $\sum_j |\text{fiber}_j(f)| = n$. This is the combinatorial partition of unity — every person belongs to exactly one fiber (the day they are assigned to). The proof invokes Mathlib's `Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise`, which decomposes a finite set's cardinality as the sum of cardinalities of its fibers under any function into a finite codomain. This theorem is the structural backbone enabling the pigeonhole argument.

title: Generalized Pigeonhole for Birthdays
content: The central result: if $n > (k-1) \cdot d$, then every birthday assignment has a k-way coincidence. The proof proceeds by contradiction: if every fiber had fewer than $k$ elements, then $n = \sum_j |\text{fiber}_j| \le \sum_j (k-1) = (k-1) \cdot d < n$, a contradiction. This uses the fiber partition of unity and `Finset.sum_le_sum` for the pointwise bound. The argument is a clean instance of the generalized pigeonhole principle: $n$ objects in $d$ bins with each bin holding fewer than $k$ objects gives $n < kd$.

title: Concrete Pigeonhole Instances (d=365)
content: Instantiates the generalized pigeonhole for the standard 365-day calendar. For k=2 (pairwise collision), 366 people suffice — this is just the classical pigeonhole. For k=3 (triple collision), 731 people guarantee some day has 3+ birthdays (since 2×365=730). These concrete examples ground the abstract bound and show how the threshold scales linearly in $(k-1)$. The actual probabilistic thresholds are much lower: ~23 for k=2, ~88 for k=3, ~187 for k=4.

title: Classical Recovery: 2-Way = Non-Injective
content: Proves the equivalence `HasKWay f 2 ↔ ¬Function.Injective f`. Forward: a fiber with $\ge 2$ elements gives two distinct people with the same birthday, contradicting injectivity. Backward: non-injectivity gives $f(i_1) = f(i_2)$ with $i_1 \ne i_2$, so the fiber at $f(i_1)$ has $\ge 2$ elements. This connects the k-way framework to the standard birthday problem, where a collision is simply a non-injective assignment. The use of `Finset.one_lt_card` extracts witnesses from fibers of size $\ge 2$.

title: Complement Characterization: Small Fibers ↔ Injective
content: Proves the dual form: all fibers have cardinality $< 2$ if and only if the assignment is injective. This is logically equivalent to the classical recovery but stated in complement form, which is more natural for probability calculations (the 'safe' assignments are the injective ones). The forward direction shows that if every fiber has at most 1 element, any two people mapping to the same day must be the same person. The backward direction shows injectivity prevents any fiber from having 2+ elements.

title: Monotonicity in k
content: Two monotonicity results. First, if some day has at least $k$ people, it certainly has at least $k'$ people for any $k' \le k$ — a simple transitivity of $\le$. Second, the special case: any k-way coincidence with $k \ge 2$ implies a 2-way coincidence (a birthday triple implies a birthday pair). These capture the nested structure of coincidence events: higher-order coincidences are strictly stronger conditions.

title: Edge Cases: k=0 and k=1
content: Validates the definition against boundary cases. A 0-way coincidence is trivially satisfied (every fiber has $\ge 0$ elements), confirming the convention that $k=0$ is vacuous. A 1-way coincidence holds for all assignments iff $n > 0$: having at least one person guarantees some day has $\ge 1$ person. The $k=1$ proof uses `Fin.elim0` for the $n=0$ case (no functions from an empty type can satisfy the existential) and constructs a witness at $f(0)$ for $n > 0$. These edge cases serve as sanity checks on the formalization.

title: Probability Definitions: noKWaySet and probKWay
content: Defines the probability of k-way coincidences using counting over the uniform distribution on assignments. The set `noKWaySet n d k` contains all assignments where every fiber has $< k$ elements (the 'safe' assignments). The probability `probKWay n d k` equals $1 - |\text{noKWaySet}|/d^n$, counting by complement. This mirrors the classical birthday probability formula $P = 1 - d!/(d^n \cdot (d-n)!)$ for $k=2$. The definition is noncomputable because it requires deciding equality of functions.

title: Probability = 1 Under Pigeonhole
content: When $n > (k-1) \cdot d$, the probability of a k-way coincidence is exactly 1: every possible birthday assignment has a k-way coincidence, so the set of 'safe' assignments is empty. The proof shows `noKWaySet = ∅` by deriving a contradiction for any purported safe assignment via the pigeonhole theorem. This converts the combinatorial pigeonhole bound into a probabilistic certainty statement.

title: Probability Monotonicity in k
content: Two related results. First, `noKWaySet_mono` proves set inclusion: if $k' \le k$, then every assignment safe for threshold $k'$ is also safe for threshold $k$ (fewer assignments avoid a weaker coincidence). Second, `probKWay_mono_k` converts this into a probability inequality: higher $k$ gives lower coincidence probability ($P(k\text{-way}) \le P(k'\text{-way})$ when $k' \le k$). The proof uses `Finset.card_le_card` on the monotone safe sets and rational arithmetic to derive the probability bound.

title: Safe Set for k=2 Equals Injective Functions
content: Proves `noKWaySet n d 2` equals the set of injective functions `Fin n → Fin d`. This is the bridge to the classical birthday probability formula: the number of injective functions from an $n$-set to a $d$-set is the descending factorial $d \cdot (d-1) \cdots (d-n+1) = d^{\underline{n}}$, giving $P(\text{collision}) = 1 - d^{\underline{n}}/d^n$. Also includes `no_kway_iff_fibers_small`, a simple restatement of the negation of `HasKWay` as a universal bound on fiber cardinalities.

title: Counting Examples: Small Populations
content: Verifies the framework against small cases. With 1 person and $d \ge 1$ days, no 2-way coincidence is possible (the single person occupies exactly one fiber of size 1). With 0 people, every fiber is empty (`fiberAt_empty` via `Fin.elim0`), so the no-k-way set is the entire function space for any $k > 0$. These base cases confirm the definitions are well-calibrated and provide inductive anchors for potential extensions.

title: Population Bounds: n < k Implies No k-Way Coincidence
content: Proves that when $n < k$, no assignment can produce a k-way coincidence: you cannot have $k$ people at one birthday with fewer than $k$ people total. The proof bounds any fiber's cardinality by $n$ (a subset of $\text{Fin}\,n$ has at most $n$ elements), then uses $n < k$ to conclude no fiber reaches the threshold. The probabilistic corollary `probKWay_zero_of_lt` shows $P(\text{k-way}) = 0$ in this regime, since $\text{noKWaySet} = \text{Finset.univ}$ and the fraction equals 1. Uses `div_self` and `pow_ne_zero` for the rational arithmetic.
mathContext: $n < k \implies P(\text{k-way}) = 0$, since $|\text{fiber}_j(f)| \le n < k$ for all $j$
